why_how.text: Some vehicles and passengers need more than a basic license, so Missouri adds endorsements.
The school bus endorsement carries extra age, license and testing rules because children ride.

scenario.text: Ray is twenty and holds a Class E for-hire license. He wants to drive a school bus.

reasoning.text: The school bus endorsement requires drivers to be at least twenty-one.

result.text: Ray must wait until he turns twenty-one before he can receive it.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking any licensed adult can add a school bus endorsement.

correction.text: Only drivers at least twenty-one with a Class E for-hire license or a commercial license with the Passenger endorsement qualify.

memory_support.text: School bus: twenty-one plus, E or P, retest at seventy-five.

prompt.text: A twenty-four-year-old with only a regular Class F license wants a school bus endorsement. Does she qualify?

answer.text: No. She also needs a Class E for-hire license or a commercial license with the Passenger endorsement.

rationale.text: The endorsement requires age twenty-one and one of those two licenses, so age alone is not enough.

narration.text: This chapter continues the story of the Missouri driver license. Here you will learn about endorsements, renewing your license, the choices and notations you can add to your card, the ways a license can be lost, and the Graduated Driver License steps that every new teen driver follows. This first lesson covers endorsements, which allow you to drive certain vehicles or carry certain passengers. You will learn when a school bus endorsement is needed, who can get and keep it, how to add a motorcycle endorsement, and which other endorsements are reserved for commercial drivers.

title.text: When a school bus endorsement applies

lines.text: Carrying students to and from school.
Vehicle built for more than ten.

narration.text: A school bus endorsement is needed to carry students between home, school and school-sponsored events in any vehicle built for more than ten passengers. Notice that the rule depends on two things together: the purpose, which is carrying students on these trips, and the vehicle, which is one built for more than ten passengers. So a large van used for a school team trip can fall under the rule just as a yellow bus does. If you drive students on these trips in a vehicle that size, you need the endorsement, whatever the vehicle looks like.

title.text: Who can get and keep it

lines.text: Class E for-hire or commercial P.
Seventy-five plus: skills test every two years.

narration.text: Only drivers who are at least twenty-one and already hold either a Class E for-hire license or a commercial license with the Passenger endorsement can receive the school bus endorsement. Keeping it has rules too. Failing a drug, alcohol or chemical test given under school bus law can suspend the endorsement for one year. A holder who is seventy-five or older must pass school bus skills testing every two years to keep it. These extra rules exist because the driver is responsible for many children at once, so the standard is higher than for an ordinary license.

lines.text: Class E for-hire or commercial P also needed.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many learners remember the age of twenty-one and forget the license requirement. Being twenty-one or older is not enough by itself. The driver must also already carry either a Class E for-hire license or a commercial license with the Passenger endorsement. So a twenty-five-year-old with only a regular Class F license does not qualify, and neither does a twenty-year-old with a Class E license. Both conditions must be met at the same time. On a test, check the age and the license type before you decide whether someone qualifies.

lines.text: Motorcycle written, vision and sign tests.
Skills test on a motorcycle or motortricycle.
Others need a commercial license or permit.

narration.text: To add the motorcycle endorsement to an existing license, you take the motorcycle written test, the vision and road sign tests, and a skills test on a motorcycle or a motortricycle. That is a full set of tests, because riding is a different skill from driving a car. Endorsements other than school bus and motorcycle are available only to holders of a commercial driver license or a commercial learner's permit. So for a Class F driver, the two endorsements that matter are school bus, with its strict rules, and motorcycle, with its own test set.

Here is a quick check: a twenty-four-year-old who holds only a regular Class F license asks to add a school bus endorsement. Does she qualify? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. She meets the age requirement of at least twenty-one, but she also needs a Class E for-hire license or a commercial license with the Passenger endorsement. Without one of those, the school bus endorsement is not available to her. And once she does qualify, she must avoid failing any school bus drug or alcohol test, which can suspend it for a year.

lines.text: School bus: twenty-one, E or P.

narration.text: To close: a school bus endorsement is needed to carry students between home, school and school events in a vehicle built for more than ten passengers. Only drivers at least twenty-one with a Class E for-hire license or a commercial Passenger endorsement can get it. A failed school bus drug or alcohol test can suspend it for a year, and holders seventy-five or older retake skills testing every two years. The motorcycle endorsement takes its own written, vision, sign and skills tests. Other endorsements are for commercial drivers. Next, renewing on time.

why_how.text: An expired license means you may not drive, so renewing on time keeps you legal.
Knowing the renewal window helps you plan around travel and other renewals.

scenario.text: Ana's license expires in five months, and she never got a reminder in the mail.

reasoning.text: She may renew up to six months early, and renewing on time is her duty even without a reminder.

result.text: Ana renews now, taking the vision and road sign tests.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a missing reminder gives you extra time to renew.

correction.text: Renewing on time is your own duty even if no reminder arrives, and driving on a lapsed license can bring a ticket.

memory_support.text: Six months early at most, six years at most.

prompt.text: Your license expires in four months and you have no reminder. May you renew now?

answer.text: Yes. You may renew up to six months before expiration.

rationale.text: The early window is six months, and renewing on time is your duty whether or not a reminder arrives.

narration.text: This lesson covers renewing your license on time. You will learn how renewal reminders work and which permits do not get them, how to update your address so reminders reach you, how early you may renew and which tests come with every renewal, why renewing is your own responsibility, what to do if you will be away for a long time, and how long a Missouri license can last. Renewing on time matters because once a license expires you may not drive, and driving on a lapsed license can lead to a ticket for driving without a valid license.

lines.text: Reminder goes to your mailing address.
None for temporary or commercial learner permits.

narration.text: The Department mails a renewal reminder to the mailing address on your record. No reminder is sent for a temporary instruction permit or a commercial learner's permit, so holders of those permits need to track the dates themselves. If you move, you can update the address that renewal reminders go to at a local license office or online. Keeping your address current is the simplest way to make sure the reminder actually reaches you. Even so, as the next slide explains, the reminder is a courtesy, and renewing on time remains your own responsibility.

lines.text: Renew up to six months early.
Vision and road sign tests each time.
Combine with registration within six months.

narration.text: You may renew your license up to six months before it expires, and every renewal includes the vision and road sign tests. If your driver license and your vehicle registration renewal dates fall within six months of each other, both renewals may be handled in one visit, which saves a trip. A Missouri driver license can be valid for as long as six years. Once it expires, you may not drive. So the safest plan is to renew within the six-month window before expiration rather than waiting until the last day or letting it lapse.

lines.text: A lapsed license can mean a ticket.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some drivers assume that if no reminder arrives, they cannot be blamed for a lapsed license. The guide says renewing on time is your own duty, even if no reminder arrives. If you drive on a lapsed license, you can be ticketed for driving without a valid license. The reminder might go to an old address, get lost, or not be sent at all for some permits. None of that changes your duty. Keep track of your expiration date yourself, and treat any reminder you do receive as a helpful extra, not a requirement.

lines.text: Long absence from state or country.
A license office can renew early.

narration.text: If you will be away from the state or the country for a long period, a license office can grant an early renewal. This is useful for students studying abroad, travelers and others who will not be in Missouri when their license comes due. Plan ahead: ask at a license office before you leave, so your license does not expire while you are away. Combined with the normal six-month early window and the option of combining renewals, the guide gives you several ways to keep your license current without driving on an expired card.

Here is a quick check: your license expires in four months, and you have not received a renewal reminder. May you renew now, or must you wait for the reminder? Work it out before reading on. You may renew now. The guide lets you renew up to six months before your license expires, and four months is inside that window. You do not need to wait for a reminder, because renewing on time is your own duty whether or not one arrives. When you renew, expect to take the vision and road sign tests, which are part of every renewal.

lines.text: Six years at most; your duty.

narration.text: To sum up: reminders are mailed to the address on your record, except for temporary instruction permits and commercial learner's permits, and you can update your address at a license office or online. You may renew up to six months early, with the vision and road sign tests each time, and you can combine license and registration renewals that fall within six months of each other. A license can last up to six years, and an expired one cannot be used to drive. Renewing on time is your duty. Next, late renewals and special cases.

why_how.text: Letting a license lapse too long brings back tests you passed before.
Service members, lost cards and suspensions each have their own renewal rules.

scenario.text: Leo's license expired two hundred days ago, and he goes to renew it.

reasoning.text: Missing the renewal by more than one hundred eighty-four days brings back the written and driving tests.

result.text: Leo takes the written, driving, vision and road sign tests.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a service member may keep driving on an expired license until renewal.

correction.text: Service members may renew without re-examination within the allowed window, but the expired license still cannot be used to drive.

memory_support.text: More than one hundred eighty-four days late, retake it all.

prompt.text: A license expired two hundred days ago. Which tests come back when renewing?

answer.text: The written and driving tests, on top of the vision and road sign tests.

rationale.text: The guide counts six months as one hundred eighty-four days for a lapse, and two hundred days is past it.

narration.text: This lesson covers renewals that fall outside the normal routine. You will learn what happens when a license has been expired too long, how the guide counts six months for a lapsed license, the special window for service members and the mail-in option for military families, how to replace a lost, stolen or destroyed license, and whether you can renew while your license is suspended or revoked. Each of these cases has a specific rule, and the numbers are easy to mix up with similar ones elsewhere in the guide, so pay close attention to each one.

lines.text: Six months means one hundred eighty-four days.

narration.text: If you miss your renewal by more than six months after expiration, you must retake the written and driving tests, on top of the vision and road sign tests. For this rule, the guide counts six months as one hundred eighty-four days. So a license that expired two hundred days ago needs the full set of tests again, while one that expired one hundred days ago does not. The safest plan is never to let it lapse, since an expired license cannot be used to drive at any point, but if it does lapse, renew well within one hundred eighty-four days.

lines.text: Six months after discharge or ninety days after return.
Whichever comes first; no driving meanwhile.

narration.text: Service members whose license expired while they were out of state can renew without re-examination for up to six months after an honorable discharge, or within ninety days of moving back to Missouri, whichever comes first. During that time the expired license still cannot be used to drive. Members of the armed forces and their dependents may also renew by mail using the Mail-In Driver License Application, with the required documents and fees. These options recognize that military service often keeps people away from Missouri when their license comes due.

lines.text: The renewal window is not permission to drive.

narration.text: Here is the trap. The service member window lets a returning service member renew without re-examination, but it does not let them drive on the expired card in the meantime. The guide is clear that the expired license still cannot be used to drive. The same is true for anyone: a renewal window is a chance to renew easily, not permission to drive on an expired license. On a test, any answer that says a service member may keep driving until the window closes is wrong. Renew first, then drive with a valid license. Valid license first, then driving.

lines.text: Lost or stolen: get a duplicate.
Expiring within six months: renew early.

narration.text: A lost, stolen or destroyed license is replaced with a duplicate, though if it expires within six months you can renew early instead. A non-commercial driver can renew while suspended, after passing the vision and road sign tests. During a revocation, renewal is allowed only if the revocation came from refusing a chemical test. In either case, the renewed license is not handed back until the reinstatement requirements are met and the driving privilege is restored. So renewing during a suspension keeps your record current, but it does not let you drive sooner.

Here is a quick check: a driver's license expired two hundred days ago, and she goes to renew it. Which tests must she take? Work it out before reading on. She must take the written and driving tests, on top of the vision and road sign tests that come with every renewal. For a lapsed license, the guide counts six months as one hundred eighty-four days, and two hundred days is past that line. If she had renewed within one hundred eighty-four days of expiration, only the vision and road sign tests would have been required.

lines.text: Over one hundred eighty-four days: full retest.

narration.text: To close: renewing more than six months late, which the guide counts as one hundred eighty-four days, brings back the written and driving tests. Service members can renew without re-examination for six months after discharge or ninety days after returning, whichever comes first, but cannot drive on the expired card, and military families can renew by mail. Lost cards get a duplicate or early renewal. Suspended drivers can renew, but the card is held until reinstatement. Next, the choices and notations you can add to your card.

why_how.text: Your license can carry information that helps others in an emergency or recognizes your service.
The donor registry lets you record your own decision about organ and tissue donation.

scenario.text: Mia has diabetes and wants emergency responders to know quickly.

reasoning.text: A medical alert notation for listed conditions such as diabetes can go on the front of the card with a signed form, at no extra cost.

result.text: Mia signs the form and the notation is added.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the donor symbol is what enrolls you in the donor registry.

correction.text: Saying yes to the donor question enrolls you; the symbol is a separate optional choice asked about afterward.

memory_support.text: Disability on the back, medical alert on the front.

prompt.text: Where does a permanent disability indicator appear, and what does it require?

answer.text: On the back of the card, with a Physicians Statement.

rationale.text: The disability indicator goes on the back with a Physicians Statement, while a medical alert goes on the front with a signed form.

narration.text: This lesson covers the optional choices you are offered when you apply for or renew a license. You will learn how the organ and tissue donor registry works and what the donor symbol is, the donation funds the clerk asks about, the notations and indicators that can appear on your card, and what each one requires and costs. You will also learn about the federal law that keeps your records private, and the voter and Selective Service registration offered at the counter. Most of these choices are free and voluntary, but each has its own rules about where it appears and what you must bring.

lines.text: Say yes at the counter to join.
Your decision stands until you change it.

narration.text: When you answer yes to the donor question at the counter, you are added to the Missouri Organ and Tissue Donor Registry. It is a first-person consent registry, which means your own decision stands unless you change it, and it needs no consent from your family. After saying yes, you are asked whether you want the optional donor symbol. If you choose it, a red heart with a green banner appears on the front of your permit, license or nondriver ID. Neither the symbol nor enrollment in the registry costs anything, and you can request a donor sticker online later.

lines.text: Clerk asks about two donation funds.

narration.text: The clerk must also ask whether you want to give money to the organ donor fund or the blindness awareness fund. These are voluntary donations. A deaf or hard of hearing applicant may ask for a DHH notation on the card, so that emergency and police personnel can quickly recognize the need to communicate differently. This notation must be requested when you apply, so think about it before your visit. It is one of several notations meant to help responders understand a situation quickly, without the driver having to explain under stress.

lines.text: Boater safety indicator: one dollar first time.
VETERAN with a discharge document, free.
Disability indicator on the back, free.

narration.text: Several other markings can be added. A Missouri resident with a current Boating Safety Education Card may add a boater safety indicator, which costs one dollar extra the first time it is added. A veteran may have VETERAN printed on the front of the card by showing an accepted discharge document, at no extra cost. A permanent disability indicator goes on the back of the card only with a Physicians Statement, costs nothing extra, and is never required by law. A medical alert notation for listed conditions, such as diabetes, epilepsy or autism, goes on the front with a signed form, also free.

title.text: Front or back of the card

lines.text: Disability indicator: back of the card.
Medical alert: front of the card.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Two health-related markings sound alike but differ in where they appear and what they require. The permanent disability indicator goes on the back of the card and requires a Physicians Statement. The medical alert notation goes on the front of the card and requires a signed form. Both are free, and neither is ever required by law. If a question pairs the disability indicator with the front of the card, or the medical alert with a Physicians Statement, it has mixed them up. Remember: disability on the back, medical alert on the front.

lines.text: Selective Service for men eighteen to twenty-six.

narration.text: The federal Driver's Privacy Protection Act requires states to close personal information in motor vehicle and license records unless state law directs otherwise, so your details are protected. At the counter, the clerk asks whether you are registered to vote at your current address and can generate an updated voter registration for your signature. Male applicants aged eighteen to twenty-six may also register with the Selective Service when they apply for a license or permit. These options let you handle several public duties in a single visit to the license office.

Here is a quick check: a driver wants a permanent disability indicator on her license. Where on the card does it appear, and what must she provide? Work it out before reading on. The indicator goes on the back of the card, and it requires a Physicians Statement. It costs nothing extra and is never required by law. Do not confuse it with the medical alert notation, which appears on the front of the card and needs a signed form instead. Both are optional choices meant to give useful information to anyone who needs to see the card.

lines.text: Yes joins the registry; symbol optional.
Notations: know the side and the form.

narration.text: To wrap up: saying yes enrolls you in the first-person donor registry with no family consent needed, and the red heart symbol is optional and free. The clerk asks about the organ donor and blindness awareness funds. You can request a DHH notation when applying, a boater indicator for one dollar the first time, VETERAN with a discharge document, a disability indicator on the back with a Physicians Statement, and a medical alert on the front with a signed form. Records stay private, and voter and Selective Service registration are offered. Next, losing a license.

why_how.text: Knowing what can cost you a license is the best way to keep it.
Parents of drivers under eighteen have a direct say in whether a license is held.

scenario.text: Tom lets his cousin borrow his license to get into a concert.

reasoning.text: Lending your license is one of the listed grounds for losing it.

result.text: Tom's license can be suspended, revoked or denied.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking only traffic crashes and impaired driving can cost a license.

correction.text: Unpaid child support, unpaid tickets, skipping court, lending your license and stealing fuel are also grounds.

memory_support.text: Impaired, fled, lied, lent, unpaid: all can cost the license.

prompt.text: Can unpaid child support cost a driver the license?

answer.text: Yes. Unpaid child support is one of the listed grounds.

rationale.text: The grounds go beyond driving behavior and include unpaid child support, unpaid tickets and skipping court.

title.text: How a license can be lost

narration.text: This lesson covers the ways a Missouri license can be taken away. First you will learn how a parent or guardian can ask the Director of Revenue to deny a license to someone under eighteen. Then you will learn the long list of grounds for suspension, revocation or denial. Some are about dangerous driving, such as driving under the influence or leaving the scene of a crash. Others are about paperwork and obligations, such as unpaid tickets, unpaid child support or lying on an application. Knowing the full list helps you avoid surprises and protect your driving privilege.

lines.text: Parent files a form with the Director.
Denial also cancels a current license.
Lasts until eighteen or until cleared.

narration.text: A parent or guardian of an applicant under eighteen can file a form asking the Director of Revenue to deny a license. Filing it also cancels a license the minor already holds. The denial lasts until the young driver turns eighteen, or until the parent asks to clear it. This gives parents a direct way to step in if they believe their teen is not ready to drive or is driving unsafely. For teen drivers, it is a reminder that until eighteen, the privilege to drive depends partly on a parent's confidence in how you use it.

lines.text: Refusing a test, leaving a crash scene.
No accident report, lying on an application.

narration.text: A license can be suspended, revoked or denied for driving under the influence, refusing an alcohol or drug test, leaving the scene of a crash, not filing a required accident report, or lying on a license application. The list continues with failing to yield and causing injury or death, using a vehicle in a felony, causing a death in a crash, and ignoring a Driver License Bureau request to take an examination. Each of these involves either dangerous driving or a failure to cooperate with the rules that keep the system honest. Any one of them can cost you your license.

Here is the trap. Many people assume a license can only be lost for bad driving. The guide lists many grounds that have nothing to do with how you drive on a given day. A license can be lost for not keeping insurance, too many points, lending your license to someone else, skipping court or leaving tickets unpaid, unpaid child support, skipping a required ignition interlock, stealing fuel, and a minor possessing liquor. So a driver with a spotless driving record can still lose a license over unpaid support or a borrowed card. Read every scenario for these hidden grounds.

lines.text: Altering or misusing a license for alcohol.

narration.text: A few more grounds involve dishonesty. Altering your license, or using someone else's license, to buy alcohol can cost you your license. So can submitting false proof of insurance. Using a vehicle in a felony, causing a death in a crash, and ignoring a Driver License Bureau request to take an examination are also listed. Together with the earlier grounds, these show that the license depends on honesty as well as safe driving. Lying on an application or lending your card can be just as serious as some driving offenses, so treat your license as a legal document.

Here is a quick check: a driver with no tickets and no crashes falls far behind on court-ordered child support. Can that cost him his license? Work it out before reading on. The answer is yes. Unpaid child support is one of the listed grounds for suspension, revocation or denial, along with skipping court, unpaid tickets, lending your license, not keeping insurance and stealing fuel. The grounds are not limited to driving behavior. A clean driving record does not protect a license from these other obligations, so keep them in good standing.

lines.text: Driving, honesty and obligations all count.

narration.text: To close: a parent or guardian of a driver under eighteen can ask the Director of Revenue to deny or cancel the license until eighteen or until the parent clears it. A license can be lost for impaired driving, refusing a test, leaving a crash scene, no accident report or lying on an application, and also for no insurance, points, lending the card, court and ticket problems, child support, interlock violations, fuel theft, minor possession, fatal failures to yield, fake or borrowed licenses, felonies and false insurance proof. Next, the GDL permit.

why_how.text: The Graduated Driver License steps let new teen drivers build skill with supervision first.
The permit rules decide who may supervise and how much practice is needed.

scenario.text: Zoe is fifteen with a permit and wants to practice with her twenty-two-year-old cousin, who is licensed.

reasoning.text: Under sixteen, a companion who is not a listed relative, guardian or instructor must be at least twenty-five, licensed three years, with written parent permission.

result.text: Zoe practices with her mother instead until she turns sixteen.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the permit companion rule is the same before and after sixteen.

correction.text: Under sixteen the rule is stricter; from sixteen any licensed driver twenty-one or older qualifies.

memory_support.text: Under sixteen: family, instructor or twenty-five; from sixteen: twenty-one.

prompt.text: A sixteen-year-old permit holder wants to practice with a licensed twenty-two-year-old friend. Is that allowed?

answer.text: Yes. From sixteen, any licensed driver at least twenty-one may be the companion.

rationale.text: At sixteen and older the companion only needs a valid license and to be twenty-one or older.

narration.text: This lesson begins the Graduated Driver License steps, often called GDL. Missouri's GDL law makes every first-time driver under eighteen hold an instruction permit and drive with a licensed driver, then drive under restrictions on an intermediate license, before getting a full license. In this lesson you will learn about step one, the instruction permit: the tests it requires, how long it lasts, who must sign for it, who may ride along as your companion before and after age sixteen, the rules about seat belts and carrying the permit, and the forty hours of practice you need.

lines.text: Vision, road sign and written tests.

narration.text: GDL step one is the instruction permit, available at age fifteen. To get it, you pass the vision, road sign and written tests. The permit is valid for up to twelve months, depending on document verification. A parent, stepparent, legal guardian, or a certified trainer from a federal residential job training program must come to the license office to sign the permit permission statement. So bring the right adult with you on permit day. The permit can be renewed repeatedly without new written tests if you need more time before moving on to the next step.

lines.text: Or twenty-five plus, licensed three years, with permission.

narration.text: Before you turn sixteen, you may drive only with a front-seat companion who is a parent, stepparent, grandparent, legal guardian or qualified instructor, or someone at least twenty-five years old who has been licensed for at least three years and has written permission from your parent. The extra conditions on that last option make sure an outside adult is experienced and approved by your family. If a parent, stepparent, grandparent or guardian is physically disabled, he or she may name up to two people to give you behind-the-wheel instruction instead.

lines.text: Under sixteen: listed adults or twenty-five plus.
From sixteen: any licensed twenty-one plus.

narration.text: Here is the trap. The companion rule is not the same throughout the permit period. Under sixteen, a companion who is not one of the listed relatives, a guardian or a qualified instructor must be at least twenty-five, licensed three years or more, and have written parent permission. From sixteen on, any licensed driver aged twenty-one or older qualifies. So a twenty-two-year-old licensed friend cannot ride along with a fifteen-year-old, but can with a sixteen-year-old. Check the permit holder's age before deciding which rule applies to a companion.

While driving on a permit, you and all passengers must wear seat belts. You must carry the permit itself, because the exam record is not enough. Before moving to the intermediate license, your permit period must include forty hours of behind-the-wheel instruction, with at least ten of those hours after dark. The hours are given by a parent, stepparent, legal guardian or certified trainer. Night practice is required because driving after dark is harder, and new drivers need experience with headlights, glare and reduced vision before they drive with fewer limits.

Here is a quick check: a sixteen-year-old with an instruction permit wants to practice with a licensed friend who is twenty-two. Is that allowed? Work it out before reading on. The answer is yes. From age sixteen, a permit holder may drive with a front-seat companion who is at least twenty-one and holds a valid license, and the friend meets both conditions. If the permit holder were still fifteen, the friend would not qualify, because under sixteen an outside companion must be at least twenty-five, licensed three years, and have written parent permission.

lines.text: Permit at fifteen after three tests.

narration.text: To close: GDL step one is the instruction permit at fifteen, after the vision, road sign and written tests, valid up to twelve months, with an approved adult signing in person. Under sixteen, your companion must be a listed relative, guardian, qualified instructor, or a qualifying adult of twenty-five; from sixteen, any licensed driver twenty-one or older. Everyone wears a seat belt, the permit itself is carried, and you need forty practice hours with ten after dark. A disabled parent may name up to two instructors. Next, GDL steps two and three.

why_how.text: The intermediate license lets teens drive alone while limiting the riskiest situations.
The full under-twenty-one license rewards a year of clean driving.

scenario.text: Sam got his intermediate license four months ago and wants to drive three classmates to a game.

reasoning.text: In the first six months he may carry no more than one passenger under nineteen who is not immediate family.

result.text: Sam drives one classmate, and the others find another ride.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the intermediate and full license check the same driving record periods.

correction.text: The intermediate license checks traffic convictions for six months; the full license checks both alcohol and traffic for twelve months.

memory_support.text: One young rider at first, three later; two years, then three.

prompt.text: An intermediate driver has held her license for eight months. How many riders under nineteen from outside her family may she carry?

answer.text: No more than three passengers under nineteen who are not immediate family.

rationale.text: The limit rises from one in the first six months to three, and only riders under nineteen outside the family count.

narration.text: This lesson covers the second and third GDL steps. You will learn how long you must hold your permit and how the guide counts that time, what record and tests you need for the intermediate license, the passenger and nighttime limits that apply to intermediate drivers, who counts as immediate family, and how long the intermediate license lasts. Then you will learn what the full under-twenty-one license requires and how long it lasts. The numbers in this lesson are close to each other, so take each one slowly and compare the steps.

lines.text: Counted as one hundred eighty-two days.
Clean record and the driving test.

narration.text: To move to the intermediate license, you must hold your permit for at least six months, which the guide counts as one hundred eighty-two days, beginning the day after the permit was issued. GDL step two, for ages sixteen to eighteen, requires no alcohol-related convictions in the past twelve months and no traffic convictions in the past six months. An adult from the approved list must come to the license office to confirm your forty hours, and you must pass the driving test, retaking the vision, road sign and written tests if earlier results are more than a year old.

lines.text: First six months: one young passenger.

narration.text: Intermediate drivers have passenger limits. In the first six months, you may carry no more than one passenger under nineteen who is not immediate family. After the first six months, the limit becomes no more than three such passengers. Both limits count only riders younger than nineteen who are outside your immediate family. Immediate family means parents, grandparents, brothers, sisters, stepbrothers, stepsisters, and adopted or foster children living in your household. The passenger limits may not apply while the license holder is doing agricultural work.

lines.text: No driving alone one to five a.m.

narration.text: An intermediate driver may not drive alone from one in the morning to five in the morning, unless going to or from a school activity, a job or an emergency, or riding with a licensed driver twenty-one or older. Late night hours are especially risky for new drivers, which is why this limit exists. The intermediate license is valid for up to two years, depending on document verification status. That gives most teens enough time to build a clean record before moving to the full license at eighteen, without needing to renew the intermediate card.

Here is the trap. The intermediate and full licenses both look at your record, but over different periods. For the intermediate license, the guide checks for alcohol-related convictions in the past twelve months and traffic convictions in the past six months. For the full under-twenty-one license, both alcohol-related offenses and traffic convictions are checked over the last twelve months, and your privilege must not be suspended, revoked or denied when you apply. So a traffic conviction eight months ago would not block the intermediate step but would block the full license.

lines.text: Valid intermediate license and clean year.
Vision and road sign tests; up to three years.

narration.text: GDL step three is the full under-twenty-one license at age eighteen. It requires a valid intermediate license, no alcohol-related offenses or traffic convictions in the last twelve months, and passing the vision and road sign tests. Your driving privilege must not be suspended, revoked or denied when you apply. The full under-twenty-one license is valid for up to three years, depending on document verification status. Compare it with the intermediate license, which lasts up to two years, so the two validity periods are two years and then three years.

Here is a quick check: an intermediate driver has held her license for eight months. How many passengers under nineteen who are not immediate family may she carry? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no more than three. In the first six months the limit is one, and after that it becomes three. Both limits count only riders younger than nineteen who are outside the driver's immediate family, so her own brother or sister would not count toward the limit. And the passenger limits may not apply while she is doing agricultural work.

lines.text: One then three riders; one to five a.m.

narration.text: To sum up: hold your permit at least one hundred eighty-two days, then get the intermediate license with a clean record, confirmed hours and the driving test. Intermediate drivers carry one young non-family passenger in the first six months and three after, and may not drive alone from one to five in the morning except for school, work, emergencies or with a licensed adult twenty-one or older. The intermediate license lasts up to two years. At eighteen, a clean twelve months and two tests earn the full under-twenty-one license, valid up to three years.

why_how.text: New residents and first-time applicants each need the right paperwork to finish getting a license.
The written exam is a serious hurdle, so studying the guide first improves your odds.

scenario.text: Kai moves to Missouri with an out-of-state license that expired one hundred days ago.

reasoning.text: A new resident can transfer an out-of-state license that is valid or expired no more than one hundred eighty-four days.

result.text: Kai transfers his license rather than starting over.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking most people pass the written exam easily without studying.

correction.text: The guide warns that almost fifty percent of test-takers fail the written exam on the first try.

memory_support.text: Study first; almost half fail the first try.

prompt.text: A new resident's out-of-state license expired one hundred days ago. Can it be transferred?

answer.text: Yes. It is within one hundred eighty-four days of expiration.

rationale.text: A license valid or expired no more than one hundred eighty-four days can be transferred by a new resident.

narration.text: This short final lesson covers a few practical points that help you finish getting your license. You will learn when a new resident can transfer an out-of-state license, what a first-time applicant brings to show the tests were passed, which documents a driver upgrading a license takes to the testing site, and why the guide urges you to study before the written exam. These points are easy to overlook, but missing a document or skipping study time can cost you an extra trip to the license office or a failed first attempt at the test.

lines.text: Transfer if valid or recently expired.

narration.text: A new resident can transfer an out-of-state license that is valid, or that has been expired no more than one hundred eighty-four days. That saves starting over from the beginning. A first-time applicant, on the other hand, brings the Driver Examination Record showing that the required tests were passed. A driver upgrading a license takes the same document set to the Highway Patrol examination site when sitting the written, vision, road sign or driving tests. Having the right papers ready keeps each visit short and avoids being sent home to collect a missing document.

lines.text: Almost half fail the first try.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because the written test is multiple choice, many people treat it as a formality and walk in without studying. The guide warns that almost fifty percent of test-takers fail the written exam on the first try. That means about one in every two first attempts ends in a failure. Studying the guide first improves your odds. Work through every chapter, not just the parts you think will be asked, and use practice questions to find the topics you need to review again before you go to the test. Preparation is the difference.

Pull these points together with the rest of the chapter. If you are a new resident with a recent out-of-state license, you may be able to transfer it, as long as it is valid or expired no more than one hundred eighty-four days. If you are a first-time applicant, bring your Driver Examination Record. If you are upgrading, take the same documents to the Highway Patrol examination site. Before any written test, study the guide carefully, since almost half of first-time test-takers fail. Then follow the GDL steps if you are under eighteen.

Here is a quick check: a new Missouri resident holds an out-of-state license that expired one hundred days ago. Can she transfer it, or must she start over? Work it out before reading on. She can transfer it. A new resident can transfer an out-of-state license that is valid or has been expired no more than one hundred eighty-four days, and one hundred days is well within that limit. If the license had been expired longer than one hundred eighty-four days, the transfer would not be available and she would need to follow the full application path.

That completes the second license chapter. You learned about the school bus and motorcycle endorsements, renewing on time and the rules for late and special renewals, the donor registry and other card notations, the many ways a license can be lost, and the three GDL steps for drivers under eighteen. This final lesson added license transfers for new residents, the Driver Examination Record for first-time applicants, documents for upgrades, and the warning that almost half of test-takers fail the written exam the first time, so study the guide before you go.
